lessons.title: Case Study: April 2020, Negative WTI and What It Meant for MCX Crude Traders

children.text: On the evening of 20 April 2020, an Indian trader who had bought MCX crude oil the week before, at what looked like a once-in-a-generation bargain of around ₹1,500 a barrel, watched something that was supposed to be impossible. The price did not just fall to zero. It went below zero. By the time the contract settled, every long position had to pay ₹2,884 per barrel on top of losing everything they had paid. A single lot bought at ₹1,500 turned into a loss of more than ₹4.3 lakh, many times the margin posted. This lesson walks through exactly what happened, why a price can go negative, how it flowed through to MCX, and the permanent lessons every commodity trader should take from it.

body.text: A futures price is not the price of a thing. It is the price of an obligation. When holding the physical commodity becomes impossible, the obligation can be worth less than nothing, and a cash-settled contract linked to it follows it down.

children.text: Why Could the Price Go Negative?

markDefs.definition: A futures contract where anyone holding a long position at expiry must take delivery of the actual commodity, and anyone short must deliver it.
A major oil storage and pipeline hub in Oklahoma, United States, and the delivery point for NYMEX WTI crude oil futures.

children.text: NYMEX WTI is a
physically delivered
contract. Anyone still holding a long May 2020 position at expiry had to take delivery of 1,000 barrels per contract at
Cushing
, Oklahoma, and find somewhere to put it.
Demand had vanished.
Refineries were cutting runs because nobody was driving or flying.
Oil kept flowing.
Wells cannot simply be switched off and on without cost, and the OPEC+ cuts had not started.
Storage was filling up.
Tanks at Cushing and elsewhere were rapidly approaching capacity, and remaining space was booked or very expensive.
Speculators could not take delivery.
Financial traders and funds holding long May contracts had no tanks, no pipelines and no refineries.
So they paid to get out.
With a day to go before expiry, sellers vastly outnumbered buyers. Longs had to pay someone with storage to take the contract off their hands.

body.text: A negative price simply means the seller pays the buyer. For a physical product that must be stored, disposal can have a cost. On 20 April 2020, the cost of being stuck with oil you could not store was higher than the value of the oil itself.

body.title: WTI May vs June 2020 contracts, settlement prices (approximate, US dollars per barrel)

children.text: Look at the June contract on 20 April: still around $20. The collapse was concentrated in the expiring month, where the delivery problem was immediate. This was contango taken to an extreme you learned about in Chapter 2: the near month was crushed by the cost and impossibility of storage.

body.label: The exchange was ready for it
body.value: CME had warned that prices could go negative
body.context: In the days before 20 April, CME Group told market participants that its systems could handle negative prices. Many traders and even some brokers did not believe it would actually happen.

body.title: The real cause
body.question: What was the main reason the WTI May 2020 contract settled at a negative price?
options: OPEC+ announced it would increase production
Holders of expiring long contracts faced delivery obligations but storage was nearly full
The US government banned oil imports
An error in the exchange's trading systems
body.explanation: The May contract required physical delivery at Cushing. With demand collapsed and storage nearly full, longs who could not take delivery had to pay others to take their positions, pushing the price below zero.

children.text: How It Flowed Through to MCX

MCX crude oil is cash settled, so no Indian trader was ever asked to take a barrel of oil. But its final settlement price is linked to the NYMEX WTI settlement price, converted into rupees. When NYMEX went negative, so did MCX.

body.latex: \text{MCX final settlement} = \text{NYMEX WTI settlement (USD)} \times \text{RBI reference rate}
body.caption: In April 2020: minus $37.63 × about 76.64 = about minus ₹2,884 per barrel.

body.title: Convert the settlement
body.prompt: The NYMEX WTI settlement was minus $37.63 per barrel and the rupee reference rate was 76.64. What is the MCX settlement price per barrel in rupees, rounded to the nearest rupee? Enter it as a negative number.
body.explanation: Minus $37.63 × 76.64 = minus ₹2,884.0 per barrel. That became the final settlement price for MCX's April 2020 crude oil contract.

children.text: What It Meant for Traders

In the days before expiry, as crude fell towards $20 and then below, many Indian retail traders bought MCX crude, reasoning that it "could not fall much further" from around ₹1,400 to ₹1,500. Illustrative outcomes for positions still open at settlement:

body.caption: Illustrative outcomes at MCX settlement of minus ₹2,884 per barrel

cells: Long 1 lot Crude Oil Mini (10 barrels)
Long position rolled to May before expiry
Exposed to the next month, not the settlement
Avoided the negative settlement, though the next contract also fell

body.title: The bargain buyer's bill
body.prompt: A trader in Surat bought one lot of MCX Crude Oil (100 barrels) at ₹1,420 per barrel a few days before expiry and held it to the final settlement of minus ₹2,884. What was the total loss in rupees? Enter it as a negative number.
body.explanation: Price change = minus ₹2,884 minus ₹1,420 = minus ₹4,304 per barrel. × 100 barrels = minus ₹4,30,400. The loss is not just the ₹1,42,000 contract value at entry; it is that plus ₹2,88,400 more, because the price went below zero.

body.text: Losses beyond your margin are still yours. When MTM and final settlement losses exceed the money in a trading account, the account goes into debit, and the client legally owes that amount to the broker. In April 2020, some Indian traders were left with debit balances many times their account value.

children.text: Some brokers and traders questioned whether the settlement should have been allowed to go negative, but MCX settled the contract according to its specification, which linked the final price to NYMEX. Exchanges and brokers around the world, including in India, then reviewed their systems and risk controls to be ready for negative prices in future.
The shock hit far beyond India.
Interactive Brokers, a large US broker, reported a loss of roughly $88 million, after its systems could not display negative prices and many clients held long positions into settlement.

Bank of China had sold a retail product called "Crude Oil Treasure", linked to US crude futures. Investors who had not rolled their positions faced losses larger than their investment, and the bank faced public anger and later compensated some of them.
The United States Oil Fund (USO), a large oil ETF that held front-month futures, suffered heavy losses and had to overhaul how it held contracts, spreading positions across later months.
The common thread: products and platforms built on the assumption that oil could not go below zero.
What Traders Assumed vs What Was True

columns.label: What many traders assumed
points: The worst I can lose is the money I put in
Cash settlement means delivery problems do not affect me
After a 70% fall, the downside is small
I can always exit before settlement

columns.label: What was actually true
points: A futures price can go negative when the delivery obligation has a cost
Futures losses can far exceed margin and the account balance
A cash-settled contract inherits the benchmark it settles against, delivery problems included
A cheap price in a broken market can still fall a long way
Liquidity can vanish near expiry, leaving no buyer at a sensible price

children.text: The Permanent Lessons
Know what your contract settles against.
MCX crude is cash settled, but it follows NYMEX WTI, a physically delivered contract. Understand the benchmark as well as your own contract.
Do not hold expiring contracts in a stressed market.
Roll or close well before expiry, especially when the curve is in steep contango.
"Cheap" is not a risk measure.
Position size must be based on how much you can lose, not how far the price has already fallen.
Leverage turns tail events into ruin.
An event nobody thought possible cost a single-lot trader more than ₹4 lakh.
Defined-risk instruments exist for a reason.
Buying an option caps the loss at the premium paid. A long futures position has no such cap.

body.title: The broken floor
body.textWithBlank: April 2020 proved that a commodity futures price can fall below ___ when storing or taking delivery of the commodity becomes impossible.
body.explanation: The WTI May 2020 contract settled at minus $37.63, and MCX crude followed at minus ₹2,884 per barrel. Any risk plan that assumes prices cannot go below zero is incomplete.

body.title: History does not repeat, but it rhymes
body.scenario: Siddharth, a 29-year-old trader in Pune, notices that MCX crude has fallen 55% in six weeks after a global recession scare. There are two trading days left before the near-month contract expires. Storage news is alarming, but he reasons: "Oil has never stayed this low. I will buy 3 full lots of the expiring contract now and let it bounce by settlement."
body.prompt: Using what you learned from April 2020, explain the specific risks in Siddharth's plan and what a more careful trader would do.
body.modelAnswer:
Specific risks:
1. Expiry timing. He is buying the contract that is about to settle, which is exactly where April 2020's damage was concentrated. If storage is stressed, the expiring month can collapse even while later months hold up.
2. Settlement linkage. MCX crude settles against NYMEX WTI. If the WTI front month breaks down, MCX follows, regardless of how the Indian market feels.
3. Liquidity. In the final days, liquidity moves to the next month. He may not find a buyer at a sensible price if he changes his mind.
4. Size. Three full lots are 300 barrels. Every ₹1,000 fall costs ₹3,00,000, and there is no floor at zero.
5. "Has never stayed this low" is not analysis. April 2020 was also unprecedented.

A more careful trader would avoid the expiring contract entirely, express any bullish view in a later month and check the size of the calendar spread, use Crude Oil Mini or a defined-risk option such as a call, size the position on a worst-case move rather than recent history, and stay out altogether if storage data suggests delivery stress.

body.title: Expiry risk checklist for energy traders
steps: Note the exact expiry date of your contract and of the benchmark contract it settles against.
Check whether the curve is in steep contango, a sign of storage stress.
Plan to roll or close several days before expiry, when liquidity is still healthy.
Make sure your account can absorb a gap far beyond your stop-loss.
Consider options when you want exposure with a capped maximum loss.

cards.definition: Minus $37.63 per barrel on 20 April 2020, the first negative settlement for the contract.
Minus ₹2,884 per barrel, derived from the NYMEX settlement and the rupee reference rate.
The storage hub and delivery point for NYMEX WTI, where storage ran short.
The requirement for longs to take the commodity at expiry, which drove the negative price.
Money a client owes the broker when losses exceed the account balance.
About 9.7 million barrels a day, agreed on 12 April but effective only from May.

points: In April 2020, COVID destroyed oil demand faster than supply could adjust, and US storage ran short.
The physically delivered WTI May contract settled at minus $37.63 because longs had to pay others to take their delivery obligations.
MCX crude, cash settled against NYMEX WTI, settled at minus ₹2,884 per barrel on the same day.
A long lot bought at ₹1,500 lost ₹4,38,400, far more than its margin, and losses beyond the balance are owed to the broker.
Cash settlement does not isolate you from delivery problems in the benchmark contract.
Avoid expiring contracts in stressed markets, size on worst cases, and use defined-risk options when appropriate.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Historical figures are drawn from widely reported market data and some are approximate. Trader outcomes shown are illustrative. Commodity derivatives are leveraged and can cause losses larger than your initial margin.
